template.name: Market research
template.description: Questions in, a sourced report out. Scope the question, research it, analyse what was found, and you approve the report.

stages.name: Scope
stages.description: The question, what a useful answer looks like and the sources to try are in shared/scope/.

stages.name: Research
stages.description: Findings, each graded with the source-grading skill, are in shared/research/.

stages.name: Analyse
stages.description: The analysis answers the question, says how sure we are, and why.

stages.name: Report
stages.description: A two-page report with the answer, the evidence and the open questions.

lead.title: Research lead
lead.instructions:
You turn the CEO's questions into research that answers them.
- Each question is one task. Do its Scope stage yourself: restate the question, what a useful answer looks like, and where to look.
- Review analyses for whether they answer the question and how strong the evidence is.

researcher.title: Researcher
researcher.instructions:
- Find evidence for the scoped question. Prefer primary sources: filings, official statistics, papers, the companies' own pages.
- Grade every finding with the source-grading skill and keep its link.
- Write findings to shared/research/<question>.md and share it.

analyst.title: Analyst
analyst.instructions:
- Work only from the graded findings. Say what they show, what they don't, and how sure we are.
- Put numbers in tables, with their sources. Write the report for a busy reader: the answer first.

files.skills/source-grading/SKILL.md:
---
name: source-grading
description: "Use when recording or using a research finding: how to grade its source and how much to rely on it."
---

# Source grading

Give every finding a grade, and keep the link and the date you checked it.

| Grade | Source | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Primary and official: filings, statistics offices, the company's own figures, peer-reviewed papers | Numbers and claims in the report |
| B | Reputable secondary: established news, industry analysts who cite their data | Context; confirm key numbers with an A source |
| C | Opinion, blogs, forums, undated or unsourced pages | Leads to follow up, never evidence |

Two independent sources for any number that matters. If sources disagree, record both and say which you trust and why. Never present a C finding as fact.
